{{Short description|Mathematical curves that are isomorphic over algebraic closures}}
In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of  [[algebraic geometry]], an [[elliptic curve]] E over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] K  has an associated '''quadratic twist''', that is another elliptic curve which is [[isomorphism|isomorphic]] to E over an [[algebraic closure]] of K. In particular, an isomorphism between elliptic curves is an [[isogeny]] of degree 1, that is an invertible isogeny. Some curves have higher order twists such as '''cubic''' and '''quartic twists'''. The curve and its twists have the same [[j-invariant]].

Applications of twists include cryptography,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bos |first1=Joppe W. |chapter=Elliptic Curve Cryptography in Practice |date=2014 |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-662-45472-5_11 |title=Financial Cryptography and Data Security |volume=8437 |pages=157–175 |editor-last=Christin |editor-first=Nicolas |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/978-3-662-45472-5_11 |isbn=978-3-662-45471-8 |access-date=2022-04-10 |last2=Halderman |first2=J. Alex |last3=Heninger |first3=Nadia |last4=Moore |first4=Jonathan |last5=Naehrig |first5=Michael |last6=Wustrow |first6=Eric |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |editor2-last=Safavi-Naini |editor2-first=Reihaneh}}</ref> the solution of [[Diophantine equation]]s,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mazur |first1=B. |author-link=Barry Mazur |last2=Rubin |first2=K. |author-link2=Karl Rubin |date=September 2010 |title=Ranks of twists of elliptic curves and Hilbert's tenth problem |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00222-010-0252-0 |journal=Inventiones Mathematicae |language=en |volume=181 |issue=3 |pages=541–575 |arxiv=0904.3709 |bibcode=2010InMat.181..541M |doi=10.1007/s00222-010-0252-0 |s2cid=3394387 |issn=0020-9910}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Poonen |first1=Bjorn |last2=Schaefer |first2=Edward F. |last3=Stoll |first3=Michael |date=2007-03-15 |title=Twists of X(7) and primitive solutions to x<sup>2</sup>+y<sup>3</sup>=z<sup>7</sup> |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/duke-mathematical-journal/volume-137/issue-1/Twists-of-X7-and-primitive-solutions-to-x2y3z7/10.1215/S0012-7094-07-13714-1.full |journal=Duke Mathematical Journal |volume=137 |issue=1 |doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-07-13714-1 |arxiv=math/0508174 |s2cid=2326034 |issn=0012-7094}}</ref> and when generalized to [[hyperelliptic curve]]s, the study of the [[Sato–Tate conjecture]].<ref name="LLG2019">{{Cite journal |last1=Lombardo |first1=Davide |last2=Lorenzo García |first2=Elisa |date=February 2019 |title=Computing twists of hyperelliptic curves |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0021869318305404 |journal=Journal of Algebra |language=en |volume=519 |pages=474–490 |doi=10.1016/j.jalgebra.2018.08.035 |arxiv=1611.04856 |bibcode=2016arXiv161104856L|s2cid=119143097 }}</ref>

==Quadratic twist==

First assume <math>K</math> is a field of [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] different from 2. Let <math>E</math> be an [[elliptic curve]] over <math>K</math> of the form:

: <math>y^2 = x^3 + a_2 x^2 +a_4 x + a_6. \, </math>

Given <math>d\neq 0</math> not a square in <math>K</math>, the '''quadratic twist''' of <math>E</math> is the curve <math>E^d</math>, defined by the equation:

: <math>dy^2 = x^3 + a_2 x^2 + a_4 x + a_6. \, </math>

or equivalently

: <math>y^2 = x^3 + d a_2 x^2 + d^2 a_4 x + d^3 a_6. \, </math>

The two elliptic curves <math>E</math> and <math>E^d</math> are not isomorphic over <math>K</math>, but rather over the [[field extension]] <math>K(\sqrt{d})</math>. Qualitatively speaking, the arithmetic of a curve and its quadratic twist can look very different in the field <math>K</math>, while the [[complex analysis]] of the curves is the same; and so a family of curves related by twisting becomes a useful setting in which to study the arithmetic properties of elliptic curves.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rubin |first1=Karl |author-link=Karl Rubin |last2=Silverberg |first2=Alice |author-link2=Alice Silverberg |date=2002-07-08 |title=Ranks of elliptic curves |url=https://www.ams.org/bull/2002-39-04/S0273-0979-02-00952-7/ |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=455–474 |doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-02-00952-7 |issn=0273-0979 |mr=1920278|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Twists can also be defined when the base field <math>K</math> is of characteristic 2. Let <math>E</math> be an [[elliptic curve]] over <math>K</math> of the form:

: <math>y^2 + a_1 x y +a_3 y = x^3 + a_2 x^2 +a_4 x + a_6. \, </math>

Given <math>d\in K</math> such that <math>X^2+X+d</math> is an [[irreducible polynomial]] over <math>K</math>, the '''quadratic twist''' of <math>E</math> is the curve <math>E^d</math>, defined by the equation:

: <math>y^2 + a_1 x y +a_3 y = x^3 + (a_2 + d a_1^2) x^2 +a_4 x + a_6 + d a_3^2. \, </math>

The two elliptic curves <math>E</math> and <math>E^d</math> are not isomorphic over <math>K</math>, but over the [[field extension]] <math>K[X]/(X^2+X+d)</math>.

===Quadratic twist over finite fields===

If <math>K</math> is a [[finite field]] with <math>q</math> elements, then for all <math>x</math> there exist a <math>y</math> such that the point <math>(x,y)</math> belongs to <math>E</math> or <math>E^d</math> (or possibly both). In fact, if <math>(x,y)</math> is on just one of the curves, there is exactly one other <math>y'</math> on that same curve (which can happen if the characteristic is not <math>2</math>).

As a consequence, <math> |E(K)|+|E^d(K)| = 2 q+2 </math> or equivalently <math> t_{E^d} = - t_E </math>, where <math>t_E</math> is the trace of the [[Frobenius endomorphism]] of the curve.

==Quartic twist==

It is possible to "twist" elliptic curves with j-invariant equal to 1728 by quartic characters;<ref>{{cite journal |first1=F. |last1=Gouvêa |author-link1=Fernando Q. Gouvêa |year=1991 |jstor=2939253 |author-link2=Barry Mazur |title=The square-free sieve and the rank of elliptic curves |last2=Mazur |first2=B. |journal=Journal of the American Mathematical Society |volume=4 |number=1 |pages=1–23 |doi=10.1090/S0894-0347-1991-1080648-7 |url=http://www.ams.org/jams/1991-04-01/S0894-0347-1991-1080648-7/S0894-0347-1991-1080648-7.pdf}}</ref> twisting a curve <math>E</math> by a '''quartic twist''', one obtains precisely four curves: one is isomorphic to <math>E</math>, one is its quadratic twist, and only the other two are really new. Also in this case, twisted curves are isomorphic over the field extension given by the twist degree.

==Cubic twist==

Analogously to the quartic twist case, an elliptic curve over <math>K</math> with j-invariant equal to zero can be twisted by cubic characters. The curves obtained are isomorphic to the starting curve over the field extension given by the twist degree.

==Generalization==
Twists can be defined for other smooth projective curves as well. Let <math>K</math> be a field and <math>C</math> be curve over that field, i.e., a [[projective variety]] of dimension 1 over <math>K</math> that is irreducible and [[geometrically (algebraic geometry)|geometrically]] connected. Then a twist <math>C'</math> of <math>C</math> is another smooth projective curve for which there exists a <math>\bar{K}</math>-isomorphism between <math>C'</math> and <math>C</math>, where the field <math>\bar{K}</math> is the algebraic closure of <math>K</math>.<ref name="LLG2019"/>
